blocks.text: Imagine trying to fit a complex jigsaw puzzle into a limited space—this is the challenge of instruction selection and register allocation in compilers.

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore how high-level intermediate representations (IR) are mapped to machine instructions and how registers are allocated efficiently. The goal is to produce correct and optimized target code.

blocks.title: Instruction Selection
blocks.text: Instruction selection is the process of converting intermediate representation (IR) code into machine code instructions.

blocks.markdown: Instruction selection involves choosing the most appropriate machine instructions to implement each operation in the IR. This is crucial for both the correctness and efficiency of the generated code.

blocks.title: Selecting Instructions for a Three-Address Statement
blocks.prompt: Consider the IR statement `t1 = t2 + t3`. Assume the target architecture supports the `ADD` instruction which adds two registers. How would you select the appropriate instructions?

steps.text: Identify the operation in the IR statement. Here, it is addition.
Map the IR operation to the target machine's instruction set. Use the `ADD` instruction for addition.
Assign registers to operands `t2` and `t3`, and store the result in register for `t1`.
Generate the machine instruction: `ADD R1, R2, R3` where `R1`, `R2`, and `R3` are registers corresponding to `t1`, `t2`, and `t3` respectively.

blocks.answer: The machine instruction is `ADD R1, R2, R3`.

blocks.title: Register Allocation
blocks.text: Register allocation is the process of assigning a large number of target program variables onto a small number of CPU registers.

blocks.markdown: Register allocation is a critical step in code generation. It involves mapping variables to a limited number of registers, which is often modeled as a graph coloring problem.

blocks.title: Graph Coloring in Register Allocation
blocks.text: Each node in the graph represents a variable, and an edge between two nodes indicates that the variables cannot be stored in the same register.

blocks.title: Register Allocation via Graph Coloring
blocks.prompt: Given variables `a`, `b`, `c`, and `d` with interference edges between `a-b`, `b-c`, and `c-d`, how can you allocate registers if only two registers are available?

steps.text: Create an interference graph with nodes `a`, `b`, `c`, and `d`.
Attempt to color the graph using two colors (representing two registers).
Assign colors: `a` and `c` can share a register, while `b` and `d` can share another.

blocks.answer: Assign `a` and `c` to Register 1, `b` and `d` to Register 2.

blocks.title: Spilling
blocks.text: Spilling occurs when there are not enough registers to hold all the variables, forcing some variables to be stored in slower memory.

blocks.markdown: Spilling is a performance bottleneck because accessing memory is significantly slower than accessing registers. Effective register allocation aims to minimize spilling.
